title: Wire armature for poseable crochet figures
subtitle: How to insert a wire frame inside a crocheted amigurumi to make it poseable
excerpt: A wire armature is a bendable wire frame placed inside a crocheted amigurumi or stuffed figure before it is closed. The wire runs through the limbs and body, allowing the finished figure to hold poses: a standing figure whose legs support its own weight, or arms that hold a position when bent. Building the armature correctly prevents the wire from poking through the crochet fabric over time.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A bendable wire frame placed inside a crocheted figure to give it a poseable internal skeleton. The armature runs through the limbs and body and is covered with wadding before the crochet fabric is placed over it.
Soft aluminium wire used for making poseable armatures. Available in 1 to 3 mm diameters. Bends and holds its shape easily without tools, and does not snap under repeated bending like regular wire.

content.text: gives a crocheted figure a poseable internal skeleton. Without armature, amigurumi and stuffed figures rely entirely on the stiffness of the stuffing to hold their shape. With armature, the figure can stand unsupported, hold its arms in position, and be posed for photography or display. The key to a long-lasting armature is protecting the wire so it cannot work through the crochet fabric.

items.name: Aluminium armature wire, 1.5 to 2 mm diameter
items.note: Available from craft and sculpting suppliers. Do not use steel wire, which is too stiff and fatigues quickly.

items.name: Wadding or polyester toy stuffing
items.note: For wrapping the wire before inserting into the crocheted figure.

items.name: Strong thread or floral tape
items.note: For securing the wadding wrap around the wire.

items.name: The crocheted figure, partially assembled and open at one seam

content.text: to size. For a humanoid figure: one piece for both arms (long enough to span from one hand, across the shoulders, to the other hand); one piece for both legs (from one foot, up through the body, down to the other foot). Overlap the two pieces at the body and twist them together in the centre.
Fold back the raw wire ends at each hand and foot by 5 mm, then bend the folded tip flat. Sharp cut wire ends can work through crochet fabric over time; folded ends are blunt.

Wrap each section of wire with a thin layer of wadding. Use strong thread or self-adhesive floral tape to secure the wadding in place. The wadding layer pads the wire so it cannot directly contact the crochet fabric from the inside.
Feed the armature into the figure through the open seam, guiding the wire into each limb. The limbs should feel firm and hold a bent position once the armature is in place.
Fill any remaining space inside the figure with toy stuffing, then close the seam using ladder stitch through the crochet fabric.

items.symptom: The wire is poking through the crochet fabric at the hands or feet
items.cause: The wire ends were not folded back, or the wadding wrap did not cover the full length of the wire.
items.fix: Open the nearest seam. Fold the wire ends and re-wrap thoroughly with wadding. Re-close the seam.

items.symptom: The figure cannot support its own weight and topples over
items.cause: The leg wire diameter is too thin for the weight of the figure, or the wire is too short and does not reach through the feet.
items.fix: Use thicker armature wire (2.5 mm rather than 1.5 mm) for heavier figures. Add flat non-slip pads to the base of the feet.

items.symptom: The wire breaks after repeated posing
items.cause: Aluminium wire fatigues at the same bending point if bent back and forth repeatedly in the same spot.
items.fix: Vary the bending point slightly when posing. If a break occurs, cut the broken section out, overlap with a new piece of wire, twist firmly, re-wrap with wadding, and re-insert.

content.text: Build an armature for a simple 15 cm amigurumi figure before attempting a larger piece. At small scale, the wire handling is straightforward and mistakes are easy to correct. The same armature-building logic (fold ends, wrap with wadding, feed into limbs) scales directly to larger figures.
